claim: Plasmodium vivax accounts for over half the world's malaria burden outside sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Plasmodium vivax accounts for over half the world's malaria burden outside sub-Saharan Africa (Gething et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gething et al., 2012

claim: Hypnozoites are formed from sporozoites which remain dormant in hepatocytes for weeks or months before developing and causing recurrent blood stage infections called relapses.
source: Hypnozoites are formed from sporozoites, which do not develop immediately following mosquito inoculation but instead remain dormant in hepatocytes for weeks or months before developing and causing recurrent blood stage infections called relapses.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about P. vivax biology

claim: P. vivax infections in tropical regions are associated with frequent relapses with intervals as short as three weeks.
source: In general, P. vivax infections in tropical regions are associated with frequent relapses (with intervals as short as three weeks) whilst relapses in P. vivax infections from Central America, Northern India and temperate regions are associated with longer intervals from acute infection to first relapse (White, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to White, 2011

claim: Primaquine is currently the only widely available antimalarial drug for the radical cure of P. vivax infections.
source: Primaquine, an 8-aminoquinoline, is currently the only widely available antimalarial drug for the radical cure of P. vivax infections.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of antimalarial therapeutics

claim: Primaquine causes predictable oxidant haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
source: Primaquine causes predictable oxidant haemolysis in G6PD deficiency (G6PDd) one of the most common genetic abnormalities of man (Cappellini and Fiorelli, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cappellini and Fiorelli, 2008

claim: G6PD deficiency is one of the most common genetic abnormalities of man.
source: Primaquine causes predictable oxidant haemolysis in G6PD deficiency (G6PDd) one of the most common genetic abnormalities of man (Cappellini and Fiorelli, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cappellini and Fiorelli, 2008

claim: Allele frequencies for G6PD deficiency vary between 3% and 35% in populations at risk from vivax malaria throughout Asia, the Mediterranean littoral and Africa.
source: Throughout Asia, the Mediterranean littoral and Africa, allele frequencies for this enzyme deficiency vary between 3% and 35% in the populations at risk from vivax malaria (Howes et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howes et al., 2013

claim: G6PD deficiency has sex-linked inheritance, where males are either deficient or normal, and women can be deficient, normal or partially deficient in proportions determined by Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
source: As G6PDd has sex-linked inheritance, males are either deficient (hemizygotes) or normal, whereas women can be deficient (homozygotes), normal or partially deficient (heterozygotes) in proportions determined by the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
evidence: Based on established genetic principles

claim: There is substantial variability in the proportion of red cells which are deficient in individual heterozygote females due to Lyonisation.
source: Because of Lyonisation, there is substantial variability in the proportion of red cells which are deficient in individual heterozygote females (Beutler et al., 1962).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beutler et al., 1962

claim: The degree of haemolysis following primaquine depends on the dose administered and the severity of the enzyme deficiency.
source: The degree of haemolysis following primaquine depends on the dose administered and the severity of the enzyme deficiency (and in heterozygote females the proportion of erythrocytes which are deficient).
evidence: Based on established understanding of G6PD deficiency and primaquine effects

claim: More severe G6PD deficiency variants found in South East Asia and the Middle East/West Asia are generally associated with more severe haemolysis compared to the common African A- variant.
source: The more severe G6PDd variants found in South East (SE) Asia (for example, Viangchan, Mahidol, Coimbra, Union) and the Middle East/West Asia (for example, Mediterranean) are generally associated with more severe haemolysis compared to the common African A- variant.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of G6PD variant severity

claim: The recommended primaquine regimen for radical cure in SE Asia and Oceania for G6PD normal patients is 0.5 mg base/kg/day for 14 days.
source: For G6PD normal patients, the primaquine regimen for radical cure that is recommended in SE Asia and Oceania (where relapse rates are high) is 0.5 mg base/kg/day for 14 days.
evidence: Based on established treatment guidelines

claim: For patients with G6PD deficiency, a weekly dose of 0.75 mg/kg/week primaquine given for a total of 8 doses is recommended.
source: For patients with G6PDd, a weekly dose is recommended; 0.75 mg/kg/week given for a total of 8 doses.
evidence: Based on established treatment guidelines

claim: G6PD deficiency testing is not widely available despite the recent introduction of point-of-care rapid diagnostic tests.
source: Unfortunately G6PDd testing is not widely available despite the recent introduction of point-of-care rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for G6PDd.
evidence: Based on current state of diagnostic availability

claim: Current G6PD deficiency RDTs are too expensive to deploy on a wide scale and can be difficult to interpret.
source: These RDTs are currently too expensive to deploy on a wide scale and can be difficult to interpret, and thus are not generally available (Brito et al., 2016-08; Satyagraha et al., 2016; Oo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brito et al., 2016-08; Satyagraha et al., 2016; Oo et al., 2016

claim: Primaquine is commonly not given to patients to avoid the risk of haemolysis, resulting in a high burden of vivax malaria.
source: Thus, primaquine is commonly not given to patients to avoid the risk of haemolysis so the burden of vivax malaria remains high, causing considerable morbidity and economic loss (Price et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Price et al., 2007

claim: Red blood cell production in the bone marrow is regulated to maintain oxygen carrying capacity.
source: RBC production in the bone marrow is regulated to maintain oxygen carrying capacity.
evidence: Based on established physiological knowledge

claim: When haemoglobin concentration in the blood falls, RBC production is up-regulated through a process mediated largely by erythropoietin.
source: When the haemoglobin concentration in the blood falls, this reduces oxygen carriage and RBC production is up-regulated, a process mediated largely by the renal hormone, erythropoietin.
evidence: Based on established physiological knowledge

claim: Normal RBCs in healthy people have a very stable life expectancy of around 120 days.
source: Normal RBCs in healthy people have a very stable life expectancy of around 120 days.
evidence: Based on established haematological knowledge

claim: Normal RBC lifespan is well modelled by a Gumbel distribution with low variance.
source: This is well modelled by a Gumbel distribution with low variance.
evidence: Based on mathematical modelling of RBC lifespan

claim: Very young red cells (reticulocytes) have the highest G6PD activity, which declines as RBCs age.
source: In nucleated cells G6PD can be newly synthesised, but the red cells lose their nucleus before leaving the bone marrow so very young red cells (reticulocytes) have the highest G6PD activity, and this declines as the RBCs age.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of G6PD enzyme activity in RBCs

claim: In most G6PD deficiency variants, the mutant enzyme degrades more rapidly compared to the normal enzyme.
source: In most G6PDd variants, the mutant enzyme degrades more rapidly compared to the normal enzyme.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of G6PD enzyme biochemistry

claim: Older erythrocytes may have up to five times less G6PD activity than reticulocytes.
source: Older erythrocytes may have up to five times less G6PD activity than reticulocytes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of G6PD enzyme activity decline

claim: G6PD deficiency results in lowered NADPH and a reduced ability to regenerate reduced glutathione.
source: G6PDd results in lowered NADPH and a reduced ability to regenerate reduced glutathione.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge

claim: Reduced glutathione protects normal RBCs against oxidant stresses such as the haemolytic effects of primaquine metabolites and certain foods.
source: Reduced glutathione protects normal RBCs against oxidant stresses such as the haemolytic effects of primaquine metabolites and certain foods, classically fava beans.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge and supported by citations

claim: As oxidant defence reserves are used up, the aging erythrocyte becomes increasingly vulnerable to oxidant haemolysis.
source: As these non-reusable oxidant defence reserves are 'used up', the aging erythrocyte becomes increasingly vulnerable to oxidant haemolysis (Beutler et al., 1954a; Dern et al., 1954; Beutler, 2008; Recht et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beutler et al., 1954a; Dern et al., 1954; Beutler, 2008; Recht et al., 2014

claim: The degree of oxidant haemolysis depends on the genetic variant of G6PD deficiency and the age distribution of the red cell population.
source: As young red cells have more functional enzyme than older cells, the degree of oxidant haemolysis depends on the genetic variant of G6PDd and the age distribution of the red cell population.
evidence: Based on logical inference from G6PD enzyme activity patterns

claim: Once older cells have haemolysed, the remaining younger erythrocytes are essentially resistant to further damage by the same primaquine dosing regimen.
source: Once the older cells have haemolysed, the remaining younger erythrocytes are essentially resistant to further damage by the same dosing regimen (that is, drug exposure) (Beutler et al., 1954a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beutler et al., 1954a

claim: Higher primaquine doses cause further haemolysis even after older cells have been destroyed.
source: However, higher primaquine doses do cause further haemolysis.
evidence: Based on established observations of dose-dependent haemolysis

claim: Temporary primaquine insensitivity in G6PD deficient individuals with continued primaquine administration was characterised by Beutler and colleagues over sixty years ago.
source: This temporary primaquine insensitivity in G6PDd individuals with the continued primaquine administration was characterised by Beutler and colleagues in a series of studies conducted over sixty years ago (Beutler et al., 1954a,1954b, 1955; Dern et al., 1954; Beutler, 1959) and later exploited by Alving et al. to develop the once weekly regimen in G6PDd (Alving et al., 1960.)
evidence: Supported by citations to Beutler et al., 1954a,1954b, 1955; Dern et al., 1954; Beutler, 1959

claim: The once weekly primaquine regimen for G6PD deficiency was developed by Alving et al. in 1960.
source: This temporary primaquine insensitivity in G6PDd individuals with the continued primaquine administration was characterised by Beutler and colleagues in a series of studies conducted over sixty years ago (Beutler et al., 1954a,1954b, 1955; Dern et al., 1954; Beutler, 1959) and later exploited by Alving et al. to develop the once weekly regimen in G6PDd (Alving et al., 1960.)
evidence: Supported by citation to Alving et al., 1960

claim: Beutler and colleagues showed haemoglobin would first fall as a result of oxidant haemolysis and then rise despite continued exposure to the same doses of primaquine.
source: By experimenting with high-dose weekly regimens and low-dose daily regimens, Beutler and colleagues showed haemoglobin would first fall as a result of oxidant haemolysis and then rise despite continued exposure to the same doses of primaquine which had caused the initial haemolysis.
evidence: Based on historical experimental observations by Beutler and colleagues

claim: The rise in haemoglobin despite continued primaquine exposure resulted from reactive erythropoiesis that introduced a younger red cell population resistant to that primaquine dose.
source: This resulted from reactive erythropoiesis (reticulocytosis) that introduced a younger red cell population to the circulation which was essentially 'resistant' to the haemolytic effects of that primaquine dose.
evidence: Based on mechanistic understanding from historical studies

claim: Intermittent primaquine administration resulted in progressively smaller cycles of haemolysis followed by reticulocytosis as the red cell population became younger.
source: Intermittent primaquine administration resulted in progressively smaller cycles of haemolysis followed by reticulocytosis as the red cell population became younger.
evidence: Based on historical experimental observations

claim: The recommended high-dose once weekly primaquine regimen for radical cure in G6PD deficient vivax malaria patients is 8 once weekly adult doses of 45 mg.
source: These results led to a recommendation for a high-dose, once weekly primaquine regimen for radical cure in vivax malaria patients with G6PDd (8 once weekly adult doses of 45 mg) (Alving et al., 1960).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alving et al., 1960

claim: Safety of the weekly primaquine regimen was not formally assessed in more severe G6PD deficiencies.
source: Safety was not formally assessed in more severe deficiencies.
evidence: Based on review of historical studies

claim: A recent trial of weekly primaquine in vivax malaria patients with Viangchan G6PD deficiency from Cambodia showed a greater fall in haemoglobin and delayed recovery from anaemia in G6PD deficient compared to G6PD normal patients.
source: A recent trial of this regimen in vivax malaria patients with the more severe Viangchan G6PDd variant from Cambodia showed a greater fall in haemoglobin and a delayed recovery from anaemia in G6PDd compared to G6PD normal patients with one patient requiring a blood transfusion (Kheng et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kheng et al., 2015

claim: One patient in the Cambodian trial of weekly primaquine in Viangchan G6PD deficiency required a blood transfusion.
source: A recent trial of this regimen in vivax malaria patients with the more severe Viangchan G6PDd variant from Cambodia showed a greater fall in haemoglobin and a delayed recovery from anaemia in G6PDd compared to G6PD normal patients with one patient requiring a blood transfusion (Kheng et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kheng et al., 2015 and represents data from the study

claim: Weekly primaquine may not be the optimal regimen for the more severe G6PD deficiency variants prevalent outside Africa.
source: These data suggest that weekly primaquine may not be the optimal regimen for the more severe G6PDd variants prevalent outside Africa.
evidence: Inferred from the Cambodian trial data showing adverse outcomes

claim: An ascending-dose regimen of primaquine could induce a safe 'slow burn' haemolysis in individuals with severe G6PD deficiency variants.
source: Reconsideration of the detailed haematological studies that laid the foundation for the weekly regimen suggests that an ascending-dose regimen of primaquine, with a schedule that matches the dynamics of red blood cell production, could induce a safe 'slow burn' haemolysis, even in individuals with severe G6PDd variants, and would still deliver a total therapeutic dose for radical cure.
evidence: Based on speculation and inference from historical data

claim: The compartmental model reproduces the essential dynamics of the body's response to primaquine-induced haemolysis in both healthy individuals and malaria patients.
source: Although this compartmental model of RBC dynamics is highly simplified, it reproduces the essential dynamics of the body's response to primaquine-induced haemolysis in both healthy individuals and malaria patients.
evidence: Based on model validation against data

claim: At steady state, approximately 0.83% of RBCs are replaced each day.
source: At steady state, approximately 0.83% of RBCs are replaced each day and 1% of RBCs in the circulation are reticulocytes.
evidence: Based on established haematological knowledge

claim: At steady state, 1% of RBCs in the circulation are reticulocytes.
source: At steady state, approximately 0.83% of RBCs are replaced each day and 1% of RBCs in the circulation are reticulocytes.
evidence: Based on established haematological knowledge

claim: Severe acute anaemia causes reticulocytes to be released into the circulating blood at an earlier age.
source: Severe acute anaemia has two consequences in the bone marrow. Reticulocytes are released into the circulating blood at an earlier age and with increased erythropoiesis normoblasts may be released into the circulation (reported as nucleated RBCs) (Hillman, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hillman, 1969

claim: With increased erythropoiesis in severe acute anaemia, normoblasts may be released into the circulation.
source: Severe acute anaemia has two consequences in the bone marrow. Reticulocytes are released into the circulating blood at an earlier age and with increased erythropoiesis normoblasts may be released into the circulation (reported as nucleated RBCs) (Hillman, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hillman, 1969

claim: In anaemia, reticulocyte release can occur after only one day, after which the cells are reticulocytes for 3.5 days in the circulation.
source: In anaemia, release can occur after only one day (then the cells are reticulocytes for 3.5 days in the circulation).
evidence: Based on established haematological knowledge

claim: The relationship between haematocrit and haemoglobin is linear.
source: The relationship between haematocrit and haemoglobin is assumed to be linear (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008

claim: Data from Pannacciulli et al. suggest cells as young as 16 days can be lysed with a daily primaquine dose of 30 mg in the severe Mediterranean variant.
source: The data from (Pannacciulli et al., 1965) suggest cells as young as 16 days can be lysed with a daily primaquine dose of 30 mg in the severe Mediterranean variant, whereas in the less severe African A- variant haemolysis appears confined to cells older than 50 days (Beutler et al., 1954a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pannacciulli et al., 1965

claim: In the African A- variant, haemolysis appears confined to cells older than 50 days.
source: The data from (Pannacciulli et al., 1965) suggest cells as young as 16 days can be lysed with a daily primaquine dose of 30 mg in the severe Mediterranean variant, whereas in the less severe African A- variant haemolysis appears confined to cells older than 50 days (Beutler et al., 1954a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beutler et al., 1954a

claim: The Khmer soldiers in the Everett et al. study are most likely to be G6PD deficient Viangchan variant rather than Mahidol.
source: The Khmer soldiers whose data are shown in Figure 2 are incorrectly referred to by Everett et al. (1977) as G6PDd Mahidol. They are in fact most likely to be G6PDd Viangchan, as the variant was discovered some ten years later [1988]
evidence: Based on inference from timing of variant discovery and citation to Everett et al., 1977

claim: In the Cambodian study by Kheng et al., 75 patients with vivax malaria were given primaquine 0.75 base mg/kg weekly for 8 weeks.
source: In this study, 75 Cambodian patients with vivax malaria were given primaquine 0.75 base mg/kg weekly for 8 weeks.
evidence: Describes the study design from Kheng et al., 2015

claim: Of the 75 patients in the Kheng et al. study, 17 were G6PD deficient Viangchan (14 homozygous males and three heterozygous females) and 1 was a homozygous male with G6PD deficient Canton.
source: Of these, 17 were G6PDd Viangchan (14 homozygous males and three heterozygous females) and 1 was a homozygous male with G6PDd Canton.
evidence: Describes patient characteristics from Kheng et al., 2015

claim: In the Kheng et al. study, haemoglobin concentrations and reticulocyte counts were measured on days 0,1,2,3 and subsequently each week before the next dose of primaquine.
source: Haemoglobin concentrations and reticulocyte counts were measured on days 0,1,2,3 and subsequently each week, before the next dose of primaquine.
evidence: Describes the measurement schedule from Kheng et al., 2015

claim: The variation in the measurement of haemoglobin was approximately 1 g/dL.
source: The variation in the measurement of haemoglobin was approximately 1 g/dL.
evidence: Based on data analysis from the study

claim: The currently recommended dose for radical cure of vivax malaria in an adult in SE Asia and Oceania delivers 420 mg of primaquine (30 mg/d x 14 d).
source: The currently recommended dose for the radical cure of vivax malaria in an adult in SE Asia and Oceania delivers 420 mg (that is, 30 mg/d x 14 d) of primaquine and is very effective (John et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to John et al., 2012

claim: The maximum primaquine dose administered in the weekly regimen is 360 mg (8 x 45 mg).
source: The maximum primaquine dose administered in the weekly regimen is 360 mg (8 x 45 mg) but the efficacy of this regimen has only been reported in Afghan refugees in Pakistan, a country with a relatively low relapse rate (Leslie et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on treatment regimen calculation

claim: The efficacy of the weekly primaquine regimen has only been reported in Afghan refugees in Pakistan, a country with a relatively low relapse rate.
source: The maximum primaquine dose administered in the weekly regimen is 360 mg (8 x 45 mg) but the efficacy of this regimen has only been reported in Afghan refugees in Pakistan, a country with a relatively low relapse rate (Leslie et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leslie et al., 2008

claim: The ascending dose regimen would be expected to be safer than the current 14 day regimens in G6PD deficient hemizygous males and homozygous females.
source: Under all circumstances, the ascending regimen proposed here would be expected to be safer than the current 14 day regimens in G6PDd hemizygous males and homozygous females, especially the 0.5 mg/kg regimen needed for frequent relapsing P. vivax.
evidence: Based on model predictions and speculation

claim: A study in healthy G6PD deficient volunteers is essential to characterise the haemolytic response to the ascending dose regimen.
source: A study in healthy G6PDd volunteers is essential to characterise the haemolytic response.
evidence: Based on research design considerations

claim: Mathematical modelling could be readily applied to the slowly eliminated 8-aminoquinoline tafenoquine.
source: This use of mathematical modelling such as this could also be readily applied to the slowly eliminated 8-aminoquinoline tafenoquine, currently being tested for safety and efficacy in humans (Beck et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beck et al., 2016 and speculation about model application

claim: Tafenoquine has the advantage of being administered as a single dose for radical cure due to its long terminal elimination half-life.
source: Tafenoquine has the great advantage of being administered as a single dose for radical cure due to its long terminal elimination half-life.
evidence: Based on established pharmacological knowledge of tafenoquine

claim: The rapidly eliminated primaquine can be stopped if there is significant haemolysis, limiting the haemolytic effect.
source: Whereas the rapidly eliminated primaquine can be stopped if there is significant haemolysis, limiting the haemolytic effect, the haemolytic effect of the slowly eliminated tafenoquine cannot be readily reversed and so haemolysis will continue until all susceptible red cells are destroyed.
evidence: Based on pharmacological reasoning about drug elimination

claim: The haemolytic effect of the slowly eliminated tafenoquine cannot be readily reversed and haemolysis will continue until all susceptible red cells are destroyed.
source: Whereas the rapidly eliminated primaquine can be stopped if there is significant haemolysis, limiting the haemolytic effect, the haemolytic effect of the slowly eliminated tafenoquine cannot be readily reversed and so haemolysis will continue until all susceptible red cells are destroyed.
evidence: Based on pharmacological reasoning about drug elimination

claim: Combined regimens for G6PD deficient patients in which primaquine is given initially to induce controlled haemolysis followed by tafenoquine might be possible.
source: Combined regimens for G6PDd patients in which primaquine is given initially to induce controlled haemolysis followed by tafenoquine might be possible, and would allow shorter total treatment durations.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential treatment strategies

claim: An ascending primaquine dose regimen for vivax radical cure might be well tolerated and effective in mild or moderately severe G6PD deficiency variants.
source: In conclusion, these results suggest that an ascending PQ dosing regimen for vivax radical cure might be well tolerated and effective in mild or moderately severe G6PDd variants.
evidence: Based on model predictions and speculation

claim: The model predictions should be tested in an adaptive phase I study.
source: These predictions should now be tested in an adaptive phase I study.
evidence: Based on research recommendations

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio in the reticulocyte data is low.
source: The signal-to-noise ratio in the reticulocyte data is low and this is apparent from the median reticulocyte count which varies considerably during the 56 days.
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 1

claim: The mechanistic model shows that a substantial rise in the reticulocyte count should occur approximately one week after the first dose, with a peak after the third dose.
source: In comparison, simulations from the mechanistic model show that a substantial rise in the reticulocyte count should occur approximately one week after the first dose, with a peak after the third dose, and then return to normal slowly over the subsequent six weeks.
evidence: Based on model simulations shown in Figure 1

claim: The serial haemoglobin data show a clear trend with a large fall after the first dose, a smaller fall after the second and then a gentle recovery with no major effect from subsequent primaquine doses.
source: The serial haemoglobin data on the other hand show a clear trend with a large fall after the first dose, a smaller fall after the second and then a gentle recovery with no major effect from subsequent primaquine doses.
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 1

claim: The model reproduces the trend in haemoglobin data and characterises satisfactorily the variance observed in steady state haemoglobin concentrations.
source: This trend is reproduced by the model and the posterior distribution also characterises satisfactorily the variance observed in steady state haemoglobin concentrations.
evidence: Based on model fit to data shown in Figure 1

claim: The deterministic compartmental model reproduces the essential patterns of observed dynamics, namely a more rapid decrease in haematocrit at the start of the regimen which then slows as haemolysis becomes self-limiting.
source: The deterministic compartmental model reproduces the essential patterns of the observed dynamics, namely, a more rapid decrease in haematocrit at the start of the regimen which then slows as the haemolysis becomes self-limiting.
evidence: Based on model fits shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: The model predicts a faster initial decrease in haemoglobin than observed for daily dosing regimens with similar nadir drop.
source: In Figure 3, for the bottom two plots, the model predicts a faster initial decrease than observed for a similar nadir drop.
evidence: Based on model fits shown in Figure 3

claim: For the mild G6PD deficiency variant, the dose-response relationship has the same shape but is shifted to the right compared to more severe variants.
source: As would be expected, for the mild variant the dose-response relationship has the same shape but is shifted to the right.
evidence: Based on dose-response analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: An adaptive design protocol has been developed to test the simplified ascending dose regimen in G6PD deficient Mahidol healthy volunteers.
source: An adaptive design protocol has been developed to test the simplified regimen (A) in G6PDd Mahidol healthy volunteers.
evidence: Based on research planning

claim: The model structure allows for simulation of the effect of malaria within an individual by altering the age distribution as P. vivax invades young erythrocytes exclusively.
source: The structure of the model also allows for the simulation of the effect of malaria within an individual by altering the age distribution as P. vivax invades young erythrocytes exclusively.
evidence: Based on model design and known biology of P. vivax

claim: It is assumed that healthy individuals with no history of haemolytic events in the last 4 months will have a uniform age distribution of RBCs.
source: It is assumed that healthy individuals with no history of haemolytic events in the last 4 months will have a uniform age distribution of RBCs.
evidence: Based on model assumption

claim: There are very few precise data on primaquine's haemolytic effect in G6PD deficient individuals despite primaquine being first tested in humans in 1944 and approved by the US FDA in 1952.
source: Although primaquine was first tested in humans in 1944 and approved by the US FDA in 1952, there are very few precise data on its haemolytic effect in G6PDd individuals.
evidence: Based on review of historical literature

claim: An exhaustive review of all available data on the haemolytic effects of primaquine has been reported by Recht et al. in 2014.
source: An exhaustive review of all available data on the haemolytic effects of primaquine has been reported recently by Recht et al. (2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Recht et al., 2014

claim: There are only five studies which present useful data on falls in haemoglobin concentrations over time following primaquine administration.
source: There are however only five studies which present useful data on falls in haemoglobin concentrations over time.
evidence: Based on review of historical literature

claim: The model fitting used Bayesian hierarchical structure for steady state haemoglobin and maximum increase in RBC production.
source: A Bayesian hierarchical structure was used for the steady state haemoglobin and the maximum increase in the production of red blood cells.
evidence: Based on model methodology

claim: The model assumes both haemoglobin levels and reticulocyte counts are observed with Laplace distributed errors.
source: The likelihood of the parameters is defined by a deterministic simulation from the compartmental model for a given dosing regimen and assumes both the haemoglobin levels and reticulocyte counts are observed with Laplace distributed errors (assuming Laplace errors is equivalent to minimizing absolute deviation).
evidence: Based on model methodology

claim: The first relapses of P. vivax emerge from the liver about 14 days after starting treatment in SE Asia and Oceania.
source: There are two reasons for this; first, adherence to long course regimens is likely to be poor, and second, the first relapses emerge from the liver about 14 days after starting treatment so the primaquine regimen has to provide sufficient drug to prevent the emergence or eliminate these parasites.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of P. vivax relapse timing

claim: The model predictions of haemolysis degree and tolerability would be expected to hold for G6PD deficiency variants with similar or less severe enzyme abnormalities than Viangchan, but not necessarily for more severe variants such as Mediterranean.
source: Thus, the model predictions of the degree of haemolysis and the tolerability and safety profile would be expected to hold for variants with similar or less severe enzyme abnormalities, but it would not necessarily hold for more severe variants such as G6PDd Mediterranean where more clinical research is required.
evidence: Based on model calibration and inference about generalizability
